name: Multiply two 8-term binary polynomials with 25 products (NIST open problem), or a smaller GF(2^8) AES-field multiplier circuit
compute_profile: laptop-days (flip-graph or SAT search over rank-25 decompositions); verification takes milliseconds
statement: The full product of two eight-term binary polynomials is a bilinear map with fifteen output coefficients. The supplied proposal attributes a 26-product construction and the question of 25 products to NIST's circuit-complexity project. Related sources are Find and Peralta (2019) and Covanov's exhaustive bilinear-map search. The supplied checked page could not retrieve the NIST problem listing, so its current open status still needs confirmation before attacking. A construction with at most 25 products or a checked impossibility proof answers the stated mathematical question. Reduced field multiplication is a separate partial target.
success_criterion: Success means an explicit bilinear algorithm over GF(2) for the product of two 8-term polynomials using at most 25 products, given as 0/1 matrices U (r x 8), V (r x 8) and W (15 x r), where r <= 25 (zero padding to 25 rows is allowed) such that, over GF(2), sum_t U[t][i] V[t][j] W[k][t] equals 1 if i + j = k and 0 otherwise, for all 0 <= i, j <= 7 and 0 <= k <= 14 (direction: min; best known 26), answering the open problem stated on https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/circuit-complexity, provided no publication has already given such an algorithm or proved it impossible (the claimant searches the literature, including doi:10.1109/TC.2018.2874662 and doi:10.1007/978-3-030-34029-2_22). The other answer also settles the open problem: CONFIRMED equally by a proof that no bilinear algorithm over GF(2) with at most 25 products exists for this map, given as a proof object accepted by a formally verified checker (for example an LRAT proof checked by cake_lpr, or a VeriPB proof checked through CakePB) for an encoding of rank-25 decompositions whose correctness is argued in a short note that a skeptic checks against the definition. Include the best valid composition of published objects for the same parameters and metric in the bar, even if it is absent from a printed table. State whether the candidate is a composition. Identify its components and composition rule. Values in unmerged pull requests are not bars.

partial_wins.statement: A circuit of 2-input AND, XOR and XNOR gates (no other gates, no constants) for multiplication in GF(2^8) modulo the AES polynomial x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1, standard polynomial basis in and out, verified on all 65536 input pairs, with at most 116 gates, i.e. strictly below the 117-gate circuit on the NIST list of circuits and below any smaller published one.

The same kind of circuit for GF(2^7) modulo x^7 + x^4 + 1 with at most 83 gates, or modulo x^7 + x^3 + 1 with at most 84, or for GF(2^6) modulo x^6 + x^3 + 1 with at most 56, verified on all input pairs and below any smaller published circuit.

A computational (not certified) answer that 26 is optimal: two independently written exhaustive searches over rank-25 bilinear decompositions of the 8-term product over GF(2), with stated symmetry reductions proved in a short note, that both complete with no solution and that a skeptic can re-run; labelled computational.

verification_method: Main claim: check the 8 x 8 x 15 tensor identity over GF(2) from U, V and W (960 equations), count the rows of U and V, and as an end-to-end check build the induced circuit and compare with schoolbook multiplication on all 2^16 pairs of 8-bit polynomials. Partial wins: parse the gate list, reject any gate other than AND, XOR, XNOR, evaluate all input pairs against a reference field multiplication (2^16 pairs for GF(2^8), 2^14 for GF(2^7), 2^12 for GF(2^6)), and count gates with the same counter applied to the NIST circuit files (data/slp/gf in github.com/usnistgov/Circuits). Milliseconds. Recompute comparison compositions using the same checker and resource metric.
status_checked: 2026-10-14; historical source check from supplied batch A material. Current sources were not re-fetched during preparation.
angles: Flip-graph random walks (Kauers-Moosbauer style) on the 8 x 8 x 15 multiplication tensor over GF(2), started from many 26-term decompositions (two-level Karatsuba variants, Chinese-remainder constructions, the published formula), looking for a reduction step; quotient by the tensor's symmetries (swapping a and b, reversing coefficient order).

SAT or MaxSAT encoding of a rank-25 decomposition with symmetry breaking (fix the first products up to the symmetry group); try restricted families first (decompositions containing many rank-one 'evaluation' products), remembering that a negative answer inside a restricted family proves nothing.

Smaller sizes first: reproduce the best published formulas for 5-, 6- and 7-term products (Montgomery 2005; Barbulescu et al. 2012) with the same search, and study what their decompositions share, before searching at 8 terms.

For the field multipliers, optimise the polynomial product and the reduction modulo the field polynomial jointly (the reduction is a fixed linear map, so merge it into the post-processing XOR layer of the bilinear algorithm and run exact or randomised XOR-SLP minimisation).
pitfalls: Read Barbulescu-Detrey-Estibals-Zimmermann 2012, Covanov 2018 and doi:10.1109/TC.2018.2874662 before investing: if any proves rank 26 optimal for 8 terms, the main target is closed. BDEZ 2012 was not read for this entry; the NIST page, updated 2026-10-06, still calls the question open.

The algorithm must use GF(2) coefficients only, so that it works when the coefficients are themselves binary polynomials. Formulas over GF(4) or with other scalars, or 25-product formulas for other bilinear maps (short product, middle product, circulant product mod x^8 - 1), do not count.

For the field multipliers, inputs and outputs must be in the standard polynomial basis; a tower-field or normal-basis multiplier (such as the 106-gate tower-field GF(2^8) circuit on the CMT page) is a different function.
Gate counting: AND, XOR and XNOR each count one; NOT gates and constants are not allowed in the NIST basis.
